original_value: Electroencephalography (EEG) has relatively poor spatial resolution and may yield incorrect brain dynamics and distort topography; thus, high-density EEG systems are necessary for better analysis. Conventional methods have been proposed to solve these problems, however, they depend on parameters or brain models that are not simple to address. Therefore, new approaches are necessary to enhance EEG spatial resolution while maintaining its data properties. In this work, we investigated the super-resolution (SR) technique using deep convolutional neural networks (CNN) with simulated EEG data with white Gaussian and real brain noises, and experimental EEG data obtained during an auditory evoked potential task. SR EEG simulated data with white Gaussian noise or brain noise demonstrated a lower mean squared error and higher correlations with sensor information, and detected sources even more clearly than did low resolution (LR) EEG. In addition, experimental SR data also demonstrated far smaller errors for N1 and P2 components, and yielded reasonable localized sources, while LR data did not. We verified our proposed approach’s feasibility and efficacy, and conclude that it may be possible to explore various brain dynamics even with a small number of sensors.

result.paraphrase: Electroencephalography (EEG) has relatively poor spatial resolution and can produce inaccurate brain dynamics and distorted topography; consequently, high-density EEG systems are needed for improved analysis. Although conventional methods have been proposed to address these issues, they rely on parameters or brain models that are not easy to handle. Accordingly, new approaches are required to improve EEG spatial resolution while preserving its data properties. In this study, we examined a super-resolution (SR) technique based on deep convolutional neural networks (CNN) using simulated EEG data with white Gaussian noise and real brain noise, as well as experimental EEG data collected during an auditory evoked potential task. SR EEG simulated data with white Gaussian noise or brain noise showed lower mean squared error and higher correlations with sensor information, and identified sources more clearly than low-resolution (LR) EEG. Moreover, experimental SR data also showed much smaller errors for the N1 and P2 components and produced reasonable localized sources, whereas LR data did not. We confirmed the feasibility and effectiveness of our proposed approach and conclude that it may enable exploration of diverse brain dynamics even with a small number of sensors.
